blocks.text: Northerncore (also known as Northern English Doomer or Northern English Aesthetic) is a regional sub-genre of the global Doomer and Sovietwave aesthetic movements. Originating on TikTok and Instagram under the `#northerncore` hashtag, it focuses on the atmospheric, melancholic, and deeply grounded visual landscape of Northern England. This differs from traditional Doomerism, which often focuses purely on urban alienation, Northerncore balances bleak post-industrial gloom with strong regional pride, working-class heritage, and sprawling natural landscapes.
Origin & Online Presence

The term Northerncore gained traction across the short-form video platform TikTok during the 2020s. Popularized through micro-moodboards, slowed audio edits, and regional photography, the `#northerncore` hashtag is used to curate content capturing the gloomy, post-industrial, and rural atmosphere of Northern England, with the hashtag having 1.6M views in total. Unlike digital-only aesthetic trends, Northerncore heavily overlaps with real-world regional identity, and local heraldry, frequently featuring historical regional symbols such as the red-and-gold Northern English flag.
Visual Style

The visual imagery of Northerncore relies heavily on high-contrast, overcast, and low-light environments. The aesthetic often leans heavily to the autumn and winter. Common motifs are split between rural topographies and urban areas:
Key Motifs

Industrial & Transport: Red-brick textile mills, Industrial infrastructure, Refineries and Chemical Plants, cooling towers, pit headstocks, power pylons cutting across fields, empty bus shelters, and quiet early-morning commuter roads.
Rural & Coastal: Low-hanging mist over moorlands, wet single-track backroads, drystone walls, coastal sea walls under grey skies, and desolate winter beaches.
Domestic Realism: Rows of Victorian terraced housing, corner shops with bright halogen lights against twilight, back alleys, brutalist architecture, pit wheel monuments and damp asphalt reflections.
Clothing/Symbols: Flat caps, Juicy Tracksuits, Addidas Tracksuits, Stone Island, Foods from the North, Whippet (dog breed)
Sound, Music and Film

The auditory backbone of the aesthetic draws heavily from 1980s English post-punk, darkwave, and atmospheric indie. Audio edits typically utilize low-fidelity filters (such as radio or telephone effects) to mimic music playing through thick fog or from an old car speaker.
Associated Artists, Genres and Films
Genres: Post-punk, Darkwave, Coldwave, Slowed & Reverb, Indie Synth, Makina, Clubland Classics, Eurodance.
Key Artists: New Order, Joy Division, The Chameleons, The Cure, Sam Fender, Chernikovskaya hata, Molchat Doma, New Order, The New Monkey.
Films: The Selfish Giant, Shameless (UK), Kes (1996), Billy Elliot, Brassed off, Tyrranosaur, Brassic, Adolescence
Regional Iconography

A defining feature that separates Northerncore from other regional Doomer movements (such as Post-Soviet or Rust Belt Doomerism) is its adoption of historic regional heraldry. Visuals frequently incorporate traditional symbols, most notably the red-and-gold Northern English flag, recontextualized as modern badges of regional unity and pride.
Reception & Criticism

Similar to other Doomer and Sovietwave subgenres, the Northerncore aesthetic is also subject to certain criticism for its romanticizing of the feelings of sadness, isolation, and the decline of the region. The idea that one may romanticize the issues of economic troubles, deindustrialization, and mental illness can contribute to passiveness in community participation. On the one hand, some cultural critics point out that excessive romanticization of visual clichés associated with Northerncore could result in the oversimplification of life experiences of people living in Northern England into aestheticalized caricatures. On the other hand, some supporters see Northerncore as local art which creates awareness about the regions struggles, and often view it through nostalgia and pride.
